subject: Anaesthesia
q: In a patient with carbon monoxide poisoning, what explains a standard pulse oximeter showing a falsely normal or near-normal SpO2 despite severe tissue hypoxia?
opts: Standard 2-wavelength pulse oximetry cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin
CO causes hemolysis of red blood cells, invalidating the reading
Pulse oximeters measure only heart rate, not oxygenation
CO increases haemoglobin's oxygen affinity beyond the sensor's detectable range
why: Correct - both COHb and O2Hb absorb light similarly at the wavelengths used.
CO poisoning does not cause hemolysis.
Pulse oximeters do measure oxygen saturation via light absorption, not just heart rate.
CO does shift the Hb-O2 curve leftward, but that isn't why the oximeter itself misreads.
exp: Standard 2-wavelength pulse oximeters cannot differentiate carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so SpO2 reads falsely normal/high in CO poisoning; true oxygenation status requires co-oximetry or an arterial blood gas.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Which bedside clinical test is most commonly used to assess adequate recovery from neuromuscular blockade before extubation?
opts: Normal blood pressure and heart rate
Ability to open eyes on command
why: Haemodynamics do not reflect neuromuscular recovery.
Correct - correlates with a TOF ratio of roughly 0.7-0.8.
Can occur with significant residual paralysis - unreliable alone.
Does not correlate well with pharyngeal/respiratory muscle recovery.
exp: A sustained 5-second head lift (or hand grip/tongue depressor test) correlates with a TOF ratio of roughly 0.7-0.8 and adequate pharyngeal/respiratory muscle recovery; quantitative TOF monitoring (ratio 0.9+) is now preferred since clinical tests can still miss residual paralysis.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: In a pregnant woman (>20 weeks gestation) who suffers cardiac arrest, what specific modification to standard CPR is recommended to improve venous return?
opts: Withhold chest compressions until delivery is achieved
Compress at a slower rate than standard
Position the patient fully upright for compressions
Manual left uterine displacement (or 15-30 degree left lateral tilt) during chest compressions
why: Compressions must start immediately - delay is dangerous.
Standard rate of 100-120/min is maintained.
Upright positioning is not used and worsens compression effectiveness.
Correct - relieves aortocaval compression, improving venous return.
exp: Beyond 20 weeks, the gravid uterus compresses the IVC/aorta in the supine position, reducing venous return and cardiac output during CPR; continuous manual left uterine displacement is recommended, with perimortem caesarean considered by 4-5 minutes if there is no ROSC.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Which pre-operative risk stratification tool estimates cardiac risk for non-cardiac surgery using six clinical predictors (high-risk surgery, ischemic heart disease, CHF, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-dependent diabetes, and renal insufficiency)?
opts: Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI / Lee index)
why: Reflects general physical/anaesthetic status, not a dedicated cardiac-specific tool.
The older, less-validated predecessor superseded by RCRI.
Screens for obstructive sleep apnoea risk, unrelated to cardiac risk.
Correct - the most widely validated tool for perioperative cardiac risk today.
exp: The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (Lee index) uses six predictors - high-risk surgery, ischemic heart disease, congestive heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-dependent diabetes, and renal insufficiency - and is the most widely validated tool for perioperative cardiac risk in non-cardiac surgery.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: In two-rescuer infant CPR, the recommended chest compression-to-ventilation ratio is:
why: The single-rescuer/adult ratio, not the two-rescuer paediatric ratio
Correct - AHA two-rescuer infant/child ratio
Used in neonatal resuscitation, not general infant CPR
Not a standard CPR ratio
exp: Two-rescuer infant and child CPR uses a 15:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio, reflecting greater emphasis on ventilation in paediatric arrests compared to the 30:2 single-rescuer/adult ratio.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: The gold-standard method to confirm correct endotracheal tube placement immediately after intubation is:
why: Can be misleading due to transmitted breath sounds and does not confirm tracheal placement definitively
Confirms depth/position later, not immediate placement
Correct - real-time, reliable confirmation of tracheal placement
Unreliable - fogging can occur even with oesophageal intubation
exp: Continuous waveform capnography is the gold standard for confirming and continuously monitoring correct tracheal versus oesophageal tube placement after intubation.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Reversal of non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockade with neostigmine must be co-administered with which drug to prevent bradycardia and other muscarinic side effects?
why: Reverses opioids, unrelated to neostigmine's action
Reverses benzodiazepines, unrelated
An alternative reversal agent for rocuronium/vecuronium, not paired with neostigmine
Correct - blocks neostigmine's unwanted muscarinic effects
exp: Neostigmine increases acetylcholine at both nicotinic sites (reversing blockade) and muscarinic sites (causing bradycardia, salivation); an antimuscarinic (atropine or glycopyrrolate) is always co-administered.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Inability to climb two flights of stairs or walk briskly without stopping corresponds to a functional capacity below which MET threshold, flagging higher perioperative cardiac risk?
why: Correct - the standard clinical threshold used in perioperative risk assessment
Higher than the recognised risk threshold
Higher than the recognised risk threshold
Unrealistically low, not the standard cutoff
exp: Functional capacity below 4 METs by history is an established marker of poor exercise tolerance and higher perioperative cardiovascular risk, prompting further cardiac workup before elective surgery.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Among Mapleson breathing circuits, which configuration is most efficient for spontaneous ventilation, and which for controlled ventilation, respectively?
opts: Mapleson D for spontaneous; Mapleson A for controlled
Mapleson A for spontaneous; Mapleson D for controlled
why: Reverses the correct efficient pairing
Correct - classic 'A for spontaneous, D for controlled' teaching
Mapleson B is inefficient for both compared with A/D
Mapleson E (Ayre's T-piece) is a paediatric circuit without a reservoir bag, not the efficiency answer here
exp: Mapleson A (Magill circuit) is most efficient for spontaneous ventilation, requiring the lowest fresh gas flow, while Mapleson D is most efficient for controlled ventilation - a frequently inverted, high-yield fact.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: A patient with end-stage renal disease on haemodialysis who missed his last two dialysis sessions suffers a cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity (PEA). Among the reversible H causes to consider and treat immediately, the most likely in this specific patient is:
why: Wrong - not specifically suggested by this clinical context.
Wrong - a generic consideration, not specific to missed dialysis.
Correct - missed dialysis strongly points to life-threatening hyperkalemia.
Wrong - not suggested by the scenario.
exp: The Hs and Ts mnemonic, Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion/acidosis, Hypo/hyperkalemia, Hypothermia, Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis, is used to systematically identify reversible causes of PEA/asystole; in a missed-dialysis patient, hyperkalemia should be treated empirically with IV calcium gluconate even before labs return, alongside emergent dialysis.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: A simple face mask is used to deliver supplemental oxygen to a spontaneously breathing patient. To prevent rebreathing of exhaled carbon dioxide within the mask, the minimum oxygen flow rate that must be maintained is:
why: Wrong - this range is used for nasal cannula and would cause CO2 accumulation in a simple mask.
Correct - minimum flow to flush mask dead space.
Wrong - these higher flows are used for non-rebreather masks with reservoir bags.
Wrong - these higher flows are used for non-rebreather masks with reservoir bags.
exp: Unlike a nasal cannula, usable from 1-6 L/min, or a non-rebreather mask, 10-15 L/min to keep the reservoir bag inflated, a simple face mask needs a minimum of about 5 L/min flow specifically to wash out exhaled CO2 trapped in the mask body - running it below this risks clinically significant rebreathing and hypercapnia.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: During general anaesthesia with a non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agent, depth of block is monitored using train-of-four (TOF) stimulation. The most commonly used peripheral nerve and its corresponding muscle response for this monitoring are:
why: Wrong - facial nerve/orbicularis oculi monitoring tends to overestimate recovery, used only as an alternative site.
Wrong - not a standard monitoring site.
Correct - the standard, most reliable site for clinical TOF monitoring.
Wrong - not a standard monitoring site for routine use.
exp: Train-of-four monitoring conventionally stimulates the ulnar nerve at the wrist and observes/measures adductor pollicis muscle twitch, thumb adduction; a TOF ratio of 0.9 or greater, quantitatively measured, is required before extubation to ensure adequate reversal of neuromuscular blockade and reduce residual paralysis-related complications.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: As per standard ASA pre-operative fasting guidelines for elective surgery under general anaesthesia in a healthy adult, the minimum recommended fasting period after a light meal (solids/non-human milk) before induction is:
why: Wrong - 2 hours applies to clear fluids, not solids.
Wrong - 4 hours is the guideline specifically for breast milk in infants.
Correct - 6 hours is the standard for a light meal/solids/non-human milk.
Wrong - 8 hours applies after a heavy/fatty meal.
exp: ASA fasting guidelines are meal-specific: clear fluids 2h, breast milk 4h, infant formula/non-human milk/light meal 6h, and a full/fatty meal 8h - the goal is minimising gastric volume to reduce aspiration risk during induction, and these apply to elective, not emergency, anaesthesia.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: During manual ventilation of an apnoeic patient with a self-inflating bag-valve-mask device, adding an oxygen reservoir bag along with a high oxygen inflow of 10-15 L/min allows the delivered FiO2 to approach:
why: Wrong - describes no oxygen supplementation at all.
Wrong - describes a bag-valve-mask without a reservoir.
Wrong - describes a bag-valve-mask without a reservoir.
Correct - reservoir plus high flow approaches near-100% FiO2.
exp: A self-inflating bag without a reservoir and with oxygen tubing alone delivers only 40-60% FiO2 because room air is entrained as the bag re-expands; attaching a reservoir bag/tube with adequate oxygen flow eliminates this air entrainment, enabling near 100% FiO2 delivery - an important distinction during resuscitation of a critically hypoxic patient.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: In a patient with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after cardiac arrest who remains comatose, current guidelines recommend targeted temperature management to which temperature range for at least 24 hours?
why: Correct, within both the classic and current (32-37.5C) recommended range
Too aggressive, old strict hypothermia target no longer mandated
Edge of the newer upper limit but not the classically tested figure
Fever is harmful post-arrest and must be actively avoided
exp: Post-cardiac-arrest care guidelines recommend active temperature control at a constant value in comatose post-ROSC patients for at least 24 hours; the classically taught range is 32C to 36C. The 2023 AHA/ILCOR focused update (built on the TTM2 trial, NEJM 2021) has since broadened the acceptable upper limit to 37.5C, with the core principle being active fever avoidance rather than a fixed narrow band - so 32-36C remains fully correct.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: A supraglottic airway device (laryngeal mask airway) is being considered for a patient undergoing a short elective procedure. Which statement about its use is correct?
opts: It provides a definitive protection against pulmonary aspiration
It does not protect the airway from aspiration of gastric contents
It requires paralysis for insertion routinely
It is placed below the vocal cords like an endotracheal tube
why: Wrong, no aspiration protection, it's a supraglottic device
Correct, LMA does not seal the trachea
Wrong, it can be inserted under deep sedation without paralysis, unlike ETT
Wrong, it sits above the vocal cords in the hypopharynx and doesn't enter the trachea
exp: The LMA sits in the hypopharynx overlying the laryngeal inlet and does not seal the trachea, so it does not protect against aspiration - it is contraindicated in high-aspiration-risk patients (full stomach, pregnancy, hiatus hernia) where a cuffed ETT is preferred.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: With repeated or prolonged administration of succinylcholine, the initial depolarizing (Phase I) block can transform into a block resembling a non-depolarizing agent. This is known as?
why: Wrong, fade IS present in phase II, absent fade is typical of phase I block
Wrong, unrelated NMB monitoring phenomenon
Correct, Phase II block shows TOF and tetanic fade
Wrong, not a recognized standard term for this transition
exp: Repeated or prolonged succinylcholine dosing causes desensitization block, or Phase II block, characterized by fade on train-of-four and tetanic stimulation similar to a non-depolarizing blocker, and can be partially reversed by anticholinesterases with caution.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: During pre-anaesthetic evaluation, the STOP-BANG questionnaire is primarily used to screen surgical patients for which condition that increases perioperative airway risk?
why: Wrong, IHD is assessed with tools like RCRI or METs
Wrong, unrelated
Wrong, MH is screened via personal or family anaesthetic history
Correct, STOP-BANG screens for OSA risk
exp: STOP-BANG is a validated screening tool for obstructive sleep apnea; a score of 3 or more flags high risk for OSA-related perioperative airway and respiratory complications, prompting extra vigilance with positioning, opioid-sparing analgesia, and postoperative monitoring.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Among non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents, which has the fastest onset of action, making it a preferred alternative for rapid sequence intubation when succinylcholine is contraindicated?
why: Vecuronium has a slower onset than rocuronium at standard doses
Atracurium's onset is also slower and it is notable instead for Hofmann elimination
Correct — fastest onset among non-depolarizing agents
Pancuronium has a slow onset and long duration, unsuitable for RSI
exp: Rocuronium, given at doses of 0.9-1.2 mg/kg, has the fastest onset among non-depolarizing muscle relaxants (approaching that of succinylcholine), making it preferred for rapid sequence intubation when succinylcholine is contraindicated; its effect can be rapidly reversed with sugammadex.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: As per the 2010 AHA ACLS guideline update, atropine was removed from routine use in which cardiac arrest rhythms, due to lack of evidence for benefit?
why: VF is managed with defibrillation and epinephrine/amiodarone, not atropine, in any guideline version
Pulseless VT is likewise managed with defibrillation, not atropine
Correct — the rhythms from which atropine was removed in 2010 and has stayed removed since
Atropine remains indicated here — this is not the rhythm it was removed from
exp: The 2010 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC removed atropine from the routine PEA/asystole cardiac arrest algorithm, as evidence did not support a survival benefit; this change was retained by the 2015 and 2020 updates. Atropine remains indicated for symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: As per the standard paediatric formula, what is the appropriate uncuffed endotracheal tube internal diameter (in mm) for a 4-year-old child?
why: This would be an underestimate for a 4-year-old by the standard formula
This does not match the formula's calculated value
Correct — (4/4)+4 = 5.0 mm
This overestimates the correctly calculated tube size
exp: The standard formula for uncuffed endotracheal tube internal diameter in children over 1 year is (age in years ÷ 4) + 4; for a 4-year-old this gives (4/4)+4 = 5.0 mm — a core PALS and paediatric anaesthesia calculation.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: As per standard preoperative fasting guidelines, what is the minimum recommended fasting period for clear fluids before elective surgery under general anaesthesia?
why: 8 hours applies to a full/fatty meal, not clear fluids
6 hours applies to formula milk or a light meal
4 hours applies to breast milk
Correct — the minimum for clear fluids
exp: Standard preoperative fasting guidelines recommend a minimum of 2 hours fasting for clear fluids, 4 hours for breast milk, 6 hours for formula/light meal, and 8 hours for a fatty meal — balancing aspiration risk against the harms of unnecessarily prolonged fasting, especially in children.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: For a hemodynamically unstable but still pulseful patient with sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, which mode of electrical therapy is indicated?
opts: Unsynchronized defibrillation, because it delivers a higher energy shock
Chemical cardioversion with adenosine only, avoiding electrical therapy
Precordial thump alone, without further electrical therapy
Synchronized cardioversion, timing the shock to the R wave to avoid the vulnerable T wave
why: Unsynchronized defibrillation risks inducing VF via R-on-T if used in a pulseful patient
Adenosine is used for narrow-complex SVT, not sustained monomorphic VT
A precordial thump has limited evidence and is not a substitute for definitive electrical therapy in unstable VT
Correct — the appropriate, safety-timed electrical therapy for unstable pulseful VT
exp: In a hemodynamically unstable but pulseful patient with monomorphic VT, synchronized cardioversion is indicated — timing the shock to the R wave avoids delivering energy during the vulnerable T wave, which could otherwise induce ventricular fibrillation (R-on-T phenomenon); unsynchronized defibrillation is reserved for pulseless VT/VF.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Insertion of a nasopharyngeal airway should be avoided (or used with extreme caution) in a patient with suspected which type of injury, due to reported cases of inadvertent intracranial placement?
why: Cervical spine injury affects airway positioning technique but is not a specific contraindication to the nasopharyngeal airway device itself
Simple septal deviation may make insertion technically harder but is not a safety contraindication
Mandibular fracture does not carry the intracranial placement risk described
Correct — the specific, classically taught safety contraindication
exp: Nasopharyngeal airway insertion carries a risk of inadvertent intracranial placement through a fractured cribriform plate in patients with suspected base of skull fracture (CSF rhinorrhea, raccoon eyes, Battle's sign); an oropharyngeal airway is generally preferred in this setting if tolerated.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: A Guedel oropharyngeal airway is being sized for an unconscious adult patient before bag-mask ventilation. How is the correct size estimated?
opts: From the tip of the nose to the earlobe
From the angle of the mouth to the sternal notch
From the xiphisternum to the angle of the mandible
From the corner of the mouth (or incisors) to the angle of the mandible/earlobe
why: This measurement (nose to earlobe/tragus) is used for sizing a nasopharyngeal airway, not an oropharyngeal airway.
The angle of the mouth to the sternal notch is not a recognized landmark for sizing any standard airway adjunct.
This measurement is not used for any standard airway adjunct sizing.
Correct — mouth corner/incisors to the mandibular angle or earlobe is the standard Guedel airway sizing method.
exp: The oropharyngeal (Guedel) airway is sized by measuring from the corner of the mouth (or central incisors) to the angle of the mandible or earlobe — correct sizing prevents tongue-base obstruction without stimulating the gag reflex or pressing on the epiglottis.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Which non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent is notable for its vagolytic effect, commonly causing a rise in heart rate, and is excreted primarily unchanged by the kidney?
why: Cisatracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination (organ-independent breakdown) and has minimal cardiovascular effects, unlike pancuronium.
Correct — pancuronium's hallmark is its vagolytic tachycardia and predominant renal excretion.
Rocuronium is an intermediate-acting aminosteroid with minimal cardiovascular effects, mainly hepatically eliminated.
Mivacurium is a short-acting benzylisoquinolinium agent metabolized by plasma cholinesterase, without a vagolytic effect.
exp: Pancuronium is a long-acting aminosteroid non-depolarizing blocker with a vagolytic (antimuscarinic) action at cardiac muscarinic receptors, producing tachycardia and mild hypertension — eliminated largely unchanged renally, so its action is prolonged in renal failure.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: During adult CPR, what is the recommended chest compression rate and depth per current resuscitation guidelines?
why: This rate and depth are both below current recommended targets.
This rate is too slow for effective adult CPR per current guidelines.
Correct — 100–120/min at 5–6 cm depth is the current recommended adult standard.
This rate and depth both exceed recommended limits and risk injury/incomplete recoil.
exp: Current adult CPR guidelines recommend a compression rate of 100-120/min at a depth of 5-6cm on a firm surface, allowing full chest recoil between compressions and minimizing interruptions — depth/rate outside this range are both associated with worse outcomes.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: A 60-year-old man scheduled for elective cholecystectomy has poorly controlled hypertension and stable angina limiting his exercise tolerance. Which ASA physical status classification best fits him?
why: Correct — severe but non-incapacitating systemic disease limiting daily function fits ASA III.
ASA I describes a completely healthy patient with no systemic disease, not applicable here.
ASA II describes mild, well-controlled systemic disease without functional limitation, which does not match "poorly controlled" hypertension with symptomatic angina.
ASA IV describes severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life, a step beyond this stable but limited patient.
exp: ASA III describes a patient with severe systemic disease that is not life-threatening but limits function (e.g., poorly controlled hypertension, stable angina, or diabetes with organ complications) — this classification, taken during pre-anaesthetic evaluation, correlates with anaesthetic risk and guides perioperative planning.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Before extubation, a train-of-four (TOF) monitor is used to assess residual neuromuscular blockade. A TOF ratio below what value indicates clinically significant residual paralysis and unsafe extubation?
why: A ratio cannot physiologically exceed 1.0 in a meaningful clinical sense — this value is not the threshold used.
A TOF ratio of 1.0 represents complete recovery, not the cutoff below which paralysis is considered residual.
This value is used in some older literature as a rougher clinical threshold, but 0.9 is the currently accepted safe cutoff.
Correct — TOF ratio <0.9 is the accepted threshold for clinically significant residual paralysis.
exp: A TOF ratio (fourth twitch amplitude divided by first) below 0.9 indicates clinically significant residual neuromuscular blockade, associated with impaired pharyngeal function and aspiration risk — extubation should be deferred, or reversal agents given, until TOF ratio reaches at least 0.9.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: A trauma patient develops sudden hypotension, distended neck veins, absent breath sounds on one side, and tracheal deviation during resuscitation, progressing to pulseless electrical activity. What is the immediate life-saving intervention?
why: Synchronized cardioversion is used for unstable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse, not for PEA from tension pneumothorax.
Correct — needle decompression is the immediate life-saving step for tension pneumothorax causing PEA.
Intubation alone does not relieve the intrathoracic pressure causing obstructive shock and may worsen it by increasing intrathoracic pressure further.
Fluids alone will not reverse the mechanical obstruction to venous return caused by tension pneumothorax.
exp: This picture — hypotension, distended neck veins, unilateral absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, PEA arrest — is classic tension pneumothorax, one of the reversible "Ts" of cardiac arrest; immediate needle decompression (2nd ICS midclavicular line, or 5th ICS anterior axillary line) relieves the pressure and must precede definitive chest tube placement.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Atracurium undergoes degradation independent of hepatic or renal function via which process?
why: Correct - atracurium undergoes spontaneous Hofmann elimination independent of organ function.
Ester hydrolysis by plasma cholinesterase describes succinylcholine and mivacurium metabolism.
Hepatic oxidation is relevant to drugs like vecuronium and rocuronium, not atracurium's defining pathway.
Renal excretion unchanged applies more to pancuronium or gallamine.
exp: Atracurium undergoes spontaneous, temperature- and pH-dependent Hofmann elimination plus ester hydrolysis, making its breakdown organ-independent and safe to use in hepatic or renal impairment, unlike vecuronium (hepatic) or pancuronium (renal).

subject: Anaesthesia
q: During single-rescuer paediatric basic life support, what is the recommended chest compression to ventilation ratio?
why: 15:2 applies to two-rescuer healthcare-provider paediatric CPR, not single-rescuer.
Correct - single-rescuer paediatric BLS uses a 30:2 ratio, matching adult BLS for simplicity.
5:1 is not a standard ILCOR/AHA compression:ventilation ratio.
3:1 is the ratio used in neonatal resuscitation, not paediatric BLS.
exp: For single-rescuer paediatric BLS, the recommended compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30:2, matching adult BLS to simplify lay-rescuer training; with two trained healthcare providers present it changes to 15:2 for more frequent ventilation.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: As per Indian standards, the colour coding of a medical oxygen gas cylinder is:
why: Not a recognized standard combination
Grey denotes carbon dioxide cylinders
Correct - black body with white shoulder is the medical oxygen code
Blue denotes nitrous oxide cylinders
exp: Medical oxygen cylinders in India are coded black body with a white shoulder, distinct from nitrous oxide (blue) and carbon dioxide (grey) - correct identification is a basic safety check before use.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: On direct laryngoscopy, only the epiglottis is visible with no glottic structures seen — this corresponds to which Cormack-Lehane grade?
why: Grade I = full glottis visible, easy intubation
Grade II = only the posterior commissure/part of the glottis visible
Correct — Grade III = epiglottis only, no glottic view, predicts difficult intubation
Grade IV = neither epiglottis nor glottis visible, the worst view
exp: Cormack-Lehane grading (I-IV) describes the laryngoscopic view during direct laryngoscopy: Grade III (epiglottis seen, glottis not seen) and Grade IV (neither seen) predict difficult intubation and should prompt use of an adjunct like a bougie or video laryngoscope rather than repeated blind attempts.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: What is the recommended initial shock energy for defibrillating pulseless ventricular tachycardia using a biphasic defibrillator?
why: Correct — biphasic devices are more efficient, needing lower energy than monophasic
360J is the standard energy for monophasic, not biphasic, defibrillators
50J is too low, more in the range of synchronized cardioversion of atrial arrhythmias
1000J is far in excess of safe/recommended energy
exp: Biphasic defibrillators are more efficient than monophasic devices, requiring a lower initial energy (typically 120-200J, device-dependent) versus 360J for monophasic; if the device's effective range is unknown, use 200J as a reasonable default (AHA ACLS). The exact range is device-dependent.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: A non-rebreather mask with a reservoir bag and adequate flow (10-15 L/min) can deliver an FiO2 of approximately:
why: That range fits a nasal cannula at low flows
That range fits a simple face mask roughly
This is closer to the FiO2 achieved with a poorly fitted non-rebreather, below its rated performance
Correct - roughly 80-95% with a good seal at 10-15 L/min flow
exp: A non-rebreather mask has a reservoir bag plus one-way valves that minimise (but do not fully abolish) room-air entrainment and rebreathing. At 10-15 L/min with a good facial seal it delivers roughly 80-95% FiO2 - the highest of the standard non-invasive low-flow devices - though a poor seal drops this toward 60%.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Prolonged apnea after a standard dose of succinylcholine is most often due to:
why: MH presents with hyperthermia and rigidity, not isolated prolonged apnea
Correct - deficient pseudocholinesterase fails to hydrolyze succinylcholine normally
Myasthenia mainly affects response to non-depolarizing agents
Hyperkalemia is a separate succinylcholine risk causing cardiac arrest, not prolonged apnea
exp: Scoline (succinylcholine) apnea results from genetically atypical or quantitatively deficient plasma pseudocholinesterase, which normally rapidly hydrolyzes succinylcholine - affected patients require prolonged ventilatory support; dibucaine number testing identifies the atypical genotype.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: A patient develops sudden hyperthermia, generalised muscle rigidity, and tachycardia shortly after induction with succinylcholine and a volatile anaesthetic agent. The specific antidote is:
why: Correct — dantrolene is the specific antidote for malignant hyperthermia
Neostigmine reverses non-depolarising neuromuscular blockade, unrelated to malignant hyperthermia
Sugammadex reverses rocuronium/vecuronium by encapsulation, unrelated to this condition
Naloxone reverses opioid overdose, unrelated to this presentation
exp: Malignant hyperthermia is a pharmacogenetic disorder (classically RYR1 mutations) triggered by succinylcholine and volatile anaesthetics, causing uncontrolled sarcoplasmic calcium release with sustained contraction, hypermetabolism, and hyperthermia; dantrolene inhibits calcium release through the ryanodine receptor and is the specific, life-saving antidote.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: During ongoing CPR, an end-tidal CO2 (PETCO2) persistently below 10 mmHg on capnography most reliably indicates what?
opts: Poor quality chest compressions / low cardiac output
why: ROSC is signaled by a sudden rise in PETCO2, not a persistently low value
A low PETCO2 signals inadequate, not adequate, compression-generated flow
Correct, PETCO2 reflects compression-generated pulmonary blood flow
Confirming tube placement is a one-time use, not what a persistently low trend means
exp: Continuous waveform capnography during CPR is an AHA-recommended quality metric - PETCO2 under 10 mmHg after 20 minutes of resuscitation is associated with very low likelihood of ROSC and can inform decisions about resuscitation quality/duration, distinct from its separate use confirming ET tube placement.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: In shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation after the third defibrillation attempt, which antiarrhythmic and initial IV dose is given first-line per ACLS?
why: Wrong — lidocaine is weight-based (1-1.5 mg/kg) and is the second-line alternative to amiodarone.
Wrong — 150 mg is the repeat (second) dose of amiodarone, not the initial bolus.
Wrong — magnesium is specifically for torsades de pointes/hypomagnesemia, not routine refractory VF.
Correct — the first-line, first dose of amiodarone in refractory VF/pulseless VT per ACLS.
exp: The ACLS pulseless VT/VF algorithm gives amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO bolus after the third shock unresponsive to CPR and epinephrine (a repeat dose of 150 mg may follow); lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg is an accepted alternative. Magnesium sulfate is reserved specifically for torsades de pointes, not routine refractory VF/VT.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: A patient on nasal cannula oxygen at 4 L/min has an approximate estimated FiO2 of what percentage, using the rule of thumb that FiO2 rises roughly 4% per L/min above room air?
why: Wrong — 24% approximates a flow of about 1 L/min, not 4 L/min.
Wrong — 60% is not achievable via a standard nasal cannula regardless of flow; needs a reservoir or Venturi device.
Wrong — 100% FiO2 requires a non-rebreather mask or a closed circuit, not a nasal cannula.
Correct — this approximates to roughly 36-40% using the +4%/L rule of thumb.
exp: The nasal cannula FiO2 rule of thumb is room air (21%) plus about 4% per L/min of flow. At 4 L/min: 21 + (4x4) = roughly 36-40%. This estimate holds practically for flows up to about 6 L/min, beyond which mucosal drying and diminishing returns occur — for higher or more precise FiO2 a Venturi mask or high-flow nasal cannula should be used instead.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Succinylcholine is best avoided in a patient with extensive burns beyond 24-48 hours after the injury because it can precipitate which life-threatening complication?
opts: Severe hyperkalemia from extrajunctional acetylcholine receptor upregulation
why: Correct — extrajunctional receptor upregulation causes an exaggerated hyperkalemic response.
Wrong — malignant hyperthermia is a distinct RYR1-mediated pharmacogenetic reaction, not burn-specific.
Wrong — phase II block occurs with repeated or prolonged succinylcholine dosing, a different phenomenon.
Wrong — anaphylaxis is a hypersensitivity reaction, not the burn-specific hyperkalemic risk.
exp: Denervation-like states from about 24-48 hours after burns, also spinal cord injury, prolonged immobilization, and major trauma, upregulate extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors over the muscle membrane; succinylcholine's depolarizing action at these receptors causes massive potassium efflux, producing life-threatening hyperkalemia and cardiac arrest. This risk persists until receptor upregulation resolves, roughly up to a year.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: During advanced cardiac life support for adult cardiac arrest, at what interval should intravenous epinephrine be re-administered?
opts: Only a single dose is given throughout resuscitation
why: Correct — standard ACLS protocol re-doses IV/IO epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 minutes during cardiac arrest, regardless of rhythm
Every 8-10 minutes is too infrequent and not the recommended interval
Every 1 minute is too frequent and not evidence-based
Epinephrine is repeated throughout resuscitation, not given as a single dose
exp: In cardiac arrest, whether shockable or non-shockable rhythm, IV/IO epinephrine 1 mg is given every 3-5 minutes as part of ACLS. For non-shockable rhythms (PEA/asystole), give it as soon as feasible; for shockable rhythms (VF/pulseless VT), give it after the second shock is unsuccessful, then every 3-5 minutes.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Which pre-operative airway assessment grades visible oropharyngeal structures with the seated patient's mouth open and tongue protruded?
why: Cormack-Lehane grades the laryngoscopic view during actual laryngoscopy, not a bedside pre-op test
Wilson score is a composite of weight, neck and jaw movement, receding mandible and buck teeth, not a single visibility grade
Thyromental distance is a physical measurement, not a graded view of pharyngeal structures
Correct — Mallampati classification grades oropharyngeal visibility with mouth open, tongue protruded, seated
exp: The Mallampati classification (Class I-IV) is a seated, mouth-open, tongue-protruded bedside grading of visible oropharyngeal structures used to predict difficult laryngoscopy; it is distinct from the Cormack-Lehane grade, which is only assigned during direct laryngoscopy itself.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Which drug rapidly reverses deep rocuronium-induced neuromuscular blockade by directly encapsulating the muscle relaxant molecule, rather than by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase?
exp: Sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin that selectively encapsulates rocuronium (and, less efficiently, vecuronium) in a 1:1 complex, allowing rapid reversal of even profound neuromuscular blockade. This differs fundamentally from anticholinesterases like neostigmine, which act indirectly by raising synaptic acetylcholine and cannot reliably reverse deep block or be used with benzylisoquinolinium agents effectively.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Which oxygen delivery device provides a fixed, predictable FiO2 regardless of the patient's inspiratory flow rate?
why: Nasal cannula is variable performance; FiO2 changes with breathing pattern
Simple face mask is also variable performance
Non-rebreathing mask gives high but variable FiO2 that depends on seal and inspiratory flow
Correct: the Venturi mask entrains a fixed ratio of air, giving a constant FiO2
exp: The Venturi mask uses the Bernoulli/jet-mixing principle: oxygen forced through a narrow orifice entrains a fixed, high ratio of room air, delivering a constant, colour-coded FiO2 that is independent of the patient's peak inspiratory flow. Nasal cannula and simple face mask are variable-performance devices whose delivered FiO2 changes with the patient's breathing pattern.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: In a 'cannot intubate, cannot ventilate' (CICV) emergency where supraglottic rescue has also failed, which is the definitive rescue airway technique?
opts: Repeat attempt at direct laryngoscopy with a bougie
Insertion of a second-generation supraglottic airway device
why: A nasopharyngeal airway is an adjunct for partial obstruction, not a rescue for complete CICV failure
Repeating a failed laryngoscopy technique wastes critical time instead of escalating to front-of-neck access
Correct — cricothyroidotomy is the definitive rescue step in the CICV algorithm
A supraglottic device is tried before declaring CICV; once ventilation still fails despite it, the algorithm moves to surgical airway access
exp: In a true CICV scenario, emergency cricothyroidotomy (surgical or needle) is the definitive front-of-neck-access rescue to secure oxygenation, per difficult airway society algorithms. It should not be delayed while repeating failed manoeuvres.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: Which non-depolarizing muscle relaxant is eliminated primarily by hepatic uptake and biliary excretion, leading to prolonged action in liver failure?
why: Correct — vecuronium depends on hepatobiliary clearance and accumulates in liver failure
Atracurium undergoes organ-independent Hofmann elimination, so it is not markedly affected by liver failure
Cisatracurium, like atracurium, is cleared by Hofmann elimination independent of hepatic/renal function
Mivacurium is metabolized by plasma pseudocholinesterase, not hepatic uptake
exp: Vecuronium is cleared predominantly by hepatobiliary excretion, with a smaller renal component, so its action is significantly prolonged in hepatic failure — distinct from atracurium and cisatracurium, which undergo organ-independent Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis, making them preferred in hepatic or renal failure.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: During adult CPR, once an endotracheal tube is in place, at what rate should ventilations be delivered?
opts: 2 breaths after every 30 compressions, pausing compressions
1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min), with continuous compressions
why: 30:2 with pauses applies only before an advanced airway is placed
20/min is hyperventilation, which reduces venous return and coronary perfusion
6/min under-ventilates; it is not the AHA rate
Correct — AHA 2020 adult ALS: 1 breath every 6 s, compressions not paused
exp: With an advanced airway (ETT or supraglottic device) in adult CPR, compressions become continuous at 100-120/min and ventilation is given asynchronously at 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min); faster rates raise intrathoracic pressure, cut venous return and lower coronary perfusion.

subject: Anaesthesia
q: For elective surgery, preoperative smoking cessation is most effective at reducing postoperative pulmonary complications when started how long before surgery?
opts: Cessation on the day of surgery only
why: 24 hours mainly improves carboxyhaemoglobin but is too short to reduce pulmonary complication rates
Correct — around 4 or more weeks of cessation is associated with meaningfully lower pulmonary complications
1 week is intermediate but insufficient evidence supports a complication-rate benefit at this duration
Same-day cessation provides essentially no time for secretion/ciliary recovery
exp: Meaningful reduction in postoperative pulmonary complications from smoking cessation generally requires at least 4 weeks of abstinence before surgery; shorter periods, even 24-48 hours which mainly lower carboxyhaemoglobin and improve oxygen delivery, do not achieve the same reduction in complication rates.
